scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Boy Dancers of Jagannath
This is Gotipua. 16th-17th century.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Long ago, the temples of Orissa maintained female dancers known as devadasis or mahari, who were devoted to Lord Jagannath.
Sculptures of dancers on bas-reliefs in temples across Orissa, including the Konark Sun Temple and the Jagannath Temple in Puri, demonstrate this ancient tradition.
With the decline of the mahari dancers around the 16th century during the reign of Rama Chandra Dev (who founded the Bhoi dynasty), young boy dancers stepped in to continue the devotional tradition.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Gotipua was developed as a sacred devotional practice to praise Lord Jagannath and Krishna.
Performances begin with an invocation expressing gratitude to Mother Earth, Jagannath, one's guru, and the assembled audience.

In present times, Gotipua is performed at cultural events, religious festivals, and dedicated gatherings such as the annual Gotipua Dance Festival in Bhubaneswar organised by the Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra Odissi Research Centre.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Gotipua performance features classical Odissi postures combined with intense yogic acrobatics.

It relies on two basic postures: tribhangi (where the body is held with bends at the head, torso, and knees) and chouka (a square-like stance symbolizing Jagannath), characterized by a fluid upper torso.
Performance items begin with a vandana (invocation) featuring a three-step salutation above the head, in front of the face, and at the chest.
Watch for Chouka, Tribhangi, Bandha Nrutya.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Gotipua is accompanied by traditional Odissi music, with the primary percussion instrument being the mardala (a two-headed drum).
The musical ensemble includes gini (small cymbals), harmonium, violin, bansuri (bamboo flute), and one or two vocalists, with the dancers themselves also singing the verses.
Listen for the Mardala, Gini, Harmonium, Violin.

A traditional Odissi musical ensemble led by the resonant two-headed mardala drum and metallic gini cymbals, layered with harmonium, violin, and bansuri flute, supporting vocal recitations sung by the young dancers.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Young male dancers transform into feminine figures by letting their hair grow, tying it in a knot woven with flower garlands, and decorating their faces with white and red powder, kajal eye lining, a round bindi, and sandalwood patterns unique to each school.
Palms and soles are painted with red alta liquid.
Costume pieces include a brightly colored blouse (kanchula) with shiny decorations and an embroidered silk cloth apron (nibibandha) tied at the waist.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra, a leading master of classical Odissi dance from Raghurajpur, began his artistic life as a Gotipua dancer.
Maguni Charan Das, a recipient of the Padma Shri award and the Odisha Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, was another celebrated master of the Gotipua dance.
In southern Odisha, especially in the district of Ganjam, the tradition of boy dancers performing in female attire evolved under the name Sakhi Nacha.
Gotipua originated as an offshoot of the ancient Mahari (devadasi) temple dance tradition following its 16th-century decline, and directly gave rise to modern Odissi classical dance.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The costume, jewellery, and ankle bells worn by Gotipua dancers are considered sacred. Outsiders and observers should respect the religious devotional nature of the performance, which praises Jagannath and Krishna.

wardrobe.policy: neutral dress with a respectful nod (palette and fabric only): the sources describe sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire, or the dance is sacred
wardrobe.from_sources: Young male dancers transform into feminine figures by letting their hair grow, tying it in a knot woven with flower garlands, and decorating their faces with white and red powder, kajal eye lining, a round bindi, and sandalwood patterns unique to each school. Palms and soles are painted with red alta liquid. Costume pieces include a brightly colored blouse (kanchula) with shiny decorations and an embroidered silk cloth apron (nibibandha) tied at the waist. Traditional dancers wear a pattasari (a thin fabric about 4 metres long tied tightly with equal lengths and a navel knot). Beaded jewellery—necklaces, bracelets, armbands, ear ornaments, and painted nose motifs—along with ankle bells, complete the costume, which is considered sacred.
